The use of excavated rock ("tunnel muck") would result in increased turbidity and suspended solids in the Whitewater Arm of Lake Jocassee. The impacts of this use of spoil have been discussed in section 3.1.2.3.
Applicant proposes to handle domestic wastes at the construction site by use of a portable extended aeration package plant of about 15,000 gallons per day capacity. The plant would include chlorination, final effluent filtration and associated collection system, pumps, and controls. Discharge would be made into Lake Jocassee. Impacts on water quality associated with this discharge have been discussed in Section 3.1.2.3.
3.2 OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE
3.2.1 Land Features and Uses
3.2.1.1 Scenic and Esthetic Resources
During operation, the level of the proposed upper and existing lower reservoirs would fluctuate, depending on immediate energy needs. In an operating cycle, the elevation of the upper reservoir could decrease approximately 160 vertical feet. Thus, a strip of mudflat would be visible around its periphery. This strip could vary in width up to approximately 718 feet. 1/
The lower existing reservoir, Lake Jocassee, would fluctuate very little relative to fluctuations in the proposed upper reservoir. Fluctuation would be very small in comparison to the surface area of the lower reservoir, and would not create any adverse visual impact.
Visually, the upper reservoir would be impacted because rapid changes in water levels would create conditions that are unfavorable for the establishment of shallow water vegetation, which might otherwise mitigate the appearance of mudflats. Adverse impacts result from the barren land. In total, the visual character would fluctuate along with the water level of the reservoir. The scenic and esthetic quality of the landscape would change in varying degrees
